title: How to Use MiMo-V2.6 for Computer Vision with Roboflow
summary: Try MiMo-V2.6 Flash in Roboflow Playground for OCR, counting, and visual reasoning, then pair it with RF-DETR in Workflows for defect inspection.
body_markdown:
SUMMARY


**MiMo-V2.6 Flash does well on OCR, counting, and visual reasoning. You can test it in Roboflow Playground, then add it to a Workflow with the OpenRouter block.**


[Roboflow Playground](https://roboflow.com/blog/roboflow-playground?ref=blog.roboflow.com) supports more than 130 vision models across 25 vision tasks, including MiMo-V2.6 Flash. In this article, I use Playground to test MiMo on several image-based tasks, then configure the same model in[Roboflow Workflows](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows?ref=blog.roboflow.com) .


## What Is MiMo-V2.6?


MiMo-V2.6 is Xiaomi's multimodal model family. It includes two variants:[MiMo-V2.6 Pro](https://playground.roboflow.com/models/xiaomi/mimo-v2-6-pro?ref=blog.roboflow.com) and[MiMo-V2.6 Flash](https://playground.roboflow.com/models/xiaomi/mimo-v2-6-flash?ref=blog.roboflow.com) . Both support text, images, video, and audio. Flash is the efficiency-focused version and is the main model tested in this article.


For vision tasks, MiMo works differently from a dedicated detector. A detector is designed to return object classes and locations. MiMo can read visible text, describe image content, answer questions, and understand relationships in a scene.


## Set Up MiMo-V2.6 Flash in Roboflow Playground


Choose MiMo-V2.6 Flash in Roboflow Playground and select the task you want to run. For an[OCR](https://roboflow.com/blog/ocr-api?ref=blog.roboflow.com) test, select OCR and upload the image. The model processes the image directly and returns the detected text.


Playground lets you run the same task with different models and compare their results. The tests below focus on MiMo-V2.6 Flash.


For questions that do not fit one of the available options, switch to Open Prompt. This mode lets you upload an image and write your own instruction. I used it for the counting test and the visual reasoning test, where the model needed to answer a specific question about the scene.


### Test 1: OCR and Printed Text


I started with a simple OCR test using a bottle production image. The labels use large, front-facing text, with the lot code and expiry date clearly visible.


MiMo-V2.6 Flash read the label correctly, including LOT 241015 and EXP 2025-10-30.


For the second test, I used an industrial carton with smaller text, angled labels, barcodes, and glare on parts of the packaging.


The model still captured the main label well. It read P/N: 142-7A305 correctly, along with the serial number and lot number. It also picked up the date, pressure range, output value, and the smaller technical text near the bottom of the label.


The side label was partly captured. Its angle and partial view make some of the text unclear to check reliably. For that reason, this OCR test focused on text that could actually be read from the source image.


### Test 2: Counting and Scene Understanding


For the next test, I switched to Open Prompt and used the same bottle production image.


Prompt: How many bottles are visible on the conveyor? Briefly describe the production scene.


MiMo-V2.6 Flash counted seven bottles, which matches the image. It also described the scene as an automated orange juice bottling line and recognized the conveyor setup. The response noticed that one bottle was uncapped while the others had caps.


The scene description included one inaccurate assumption. MiMo suggested that the uncapped bottle was still in the capping stage. Since capped bottles appear on both sides of it, the image points more toward a missed capping step. The test showed that MiMo could count the bottles correctly and understand the production scene, though its explanation of the uncapped bottle needed closer checking.


### Test 3: Visual Reasoning


For the reasoning test, I kept the same production-line image and changed the question. This time, the prompt asked MiMo to find the bottle that broke the visual pattern in the row:


Prompt: Which bottle breaks the visual pattern of the row? Give its position from the left and explain the visible difference.


MiMo-V2.6 Flash correctly picked the fourth bottle from the left and identified the missing white cap as the difference. To answer the prompt, the model had to spot the anomaly and match it to a specific position in the row. The response matched what was visible in the image without adding another assumption about the production process.


## Use MiMo-V2.6 Flash in Roboflow Workflows


After testing MiMo-V2.6 Flash in Playground, the next step was to try the model in Roboflow Workflows with an[inspection task](https://roboflow.com/blog/ai-agents-for-visual-inspection?ref=blog.roboflow.com) . Playground provides a quick way to test MiMo across the available options and see how it handles different types of visual input. Workflows let the model run as part of a reusable pipeline and connect with other processing steps.


For this Workflow test, a more challenging production-line image was used with more bottles and several packaging differences.


The Workflow sends the image from the Inputs block to the[OpenRouter block](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/blocks/blocks/run-a-model/open-router?ref=blog.roboflow.com) , then returns the result through the Outputs block. In the OpenRouter settings, the model is set to xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-flash, and the task type is Open Prompt. The prompt asks MiMo to inspect each bottle for visible packaging defects and flag any issues it finds.


After running the Workflow, MiMo returned its inspection through the open_router_output field.


MiMo flagged two bottles, correctly identifying the sixth from the left as missing its cap and the eighth as having a damaged label. The next bottle had a crooked cap, but MiMo did not flag it in this full-image run.


## Add MiMo to a Multi-Stage Vision Pipeline


The[next Workflow](https://app.roboflow.com/workflows/embed/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ3b3JrZmxvd0lkIjoiY0VQc0c2dWpzOWhLRXkwTzNITlUiLCJ3b3Jrc3BhY2VJZCI6Im5JRk5DOGRjbU5OOXZ4d29ybWpoWTdCNjdQZTIiLCJ1c2VySWQiOiJuSUZOQzhkY21OTjl2eHdvcm1qaFk3QjY3UGUyIiwiaWF0IjoxNzkxMjA5NTA2fQ.pcHlRg0JUBeFLAv079669eVSg_ybRTkZFV06IjjqM3c?ref=blog.roboflow.com) adds an object detection step before MiMo so each bottle can be checked separately.


[RF-DETR Nano](https://rfdetr.roboflow.com/reference/nano/?ref=blog.roboflow.com#rfdetr.detr.RFDETRNano) first detects the bottles in the production image, then a[Dynamic Crop block](https://docs.roboflow.com/workflows/blocks/blocks/transformations/dynamic-crop?ref=blog.roboflow.com) creates one crop for each detection and passes those crops to MiMo-V2.6 Flash for inspection.


With the bottles cropped, MiMo receives one bottle at a time. The prompt asks it to check the cap and label, then return the result in the same format for every crop:


Status: PASS/FAIL | Cap: correct/missing/crooked/uncertain | Label: normal/wrinkled/torn/peeling/uncertain


MiMo correctly flagged the bottle with the missing cap and the bottle with the wrinkled label; both results matched the visible defects in the image. The other bottle crops were returned as passes. The bottle with the crooked cap was still classified as “Cap: correct” after it was cropped. MiMo missed the same defect even with a closer view.


## MiMo-V2.6 Flash vs. Pro on the Crooked-Cap Defect


The two MiMo-V2.6 variants differ a lot in size. Flash has about 309 billion total parameters, with 15 billion active per token, while Pro has 1.02 trillion total parameters, with about 42 billion active per token.


In[Roboflow’s Vision Evals](https://playground.roboflow.com/evals?ref=blog.roboflow.com) , updated October 13, 2026, Pro scored slightly higher overall than Flash at low reasoning effort. The results varied by task and reasoning setting:


Benchmark metric


MiMo-V2.6 Flash


MiMo-V2.6 Pro


Overall score, low reasoning effort


49.2%


50.3%


OCR, low reasoning effort


49.7%


48.6%


OCR, high reasoning effort


50.4%


49.9%


The OCR results are preliminary and based on a single run for each configuration. These benchmark scores provide context for comparing the models, but testing on your own images is necessary to determine whether either model can identify the defects your application needs to catch.


To check whether the larger model would handle the crooked-cap defect differently, the same multi-stage Workflow was run with xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-pro. The image and inspection prompt stayed the same, so the model was the only change.


Pro found the missing cap and damaged label. The crooked cap was again returned as Cap: correct. For this specific inspection case, switching from Flash to Pro did not fix the missed defect.


### What the MiMo-V2.6 Tests Showed


Across the tests, MiMo-V2.6 Flash performed well when the visual evidence was easy to distinguish. OCR and counting produced strong results, and the model also handled the visual reasoning prompt correctly. Errors appeared when the task depended on a smaller visual detail or when the model made assumptions beyond what the image clearly showed.


Cropping each bottle made the inspection output more structured. MiMo still missed the crooked cap, and Pro returned the same result when tested with the same setup.


## Get Started with MiMo-V2.6 Flash for Vision


MiMo-V2.6 Flash can add image understanding to a workflow alongside standard detection. Start by testing images and prompts in Playground, then move into Workflows once you understand how MiMo responds to those inputs.
